THE ORCHARD · PURCHASING-POWER EXPERIMENT

THE NUT
STANDARD

What if the economy were priced in nuts instead of dollars?

A dollar is only one ruler. Price the same economy in peanuts, almonds, hazelnuts, gold, bitcoin, productive acres, or orchard land, and the inflation story changes.

1 · nominal
$1 stays $1

The label on the money is stable. That says nothing about what it buys.

2 · real
Buying power moves

If the same basket needs more units, that unit weakened against the basket.

3 · relative
Each nut is its own market

Peanuts, almonds, pecans and pistachios do not tell the same story.

Nut prices and the cost of living do not move together.

U.S. processed nut prices (BLS Producer Price Index) versus the all-item Consumer Price Index (CPI). Both series are rebased to January 1998 = 100 so only the change matters.

Processed nut prices · BLS PPIAll-item CPIJanuary snapshots · 1998 = 100

01 · start with the claim

One economy. Many rulers.

The same economy can be quoted in dollars, nuts, gold, or bitcoin. The basket is the same. Only the ruler changes.

if priced in dollars
CPI ↑

The U.S. consumer basket became more expensive in dollars over time. That is ordinary inflation accounting.

if priced in nuts
Depends

Each nut behaves like its own small commodity currency. Some got more expensive, some cheaper, some far more volatile.

if priced in gold or bitcoin
Very different

Hard assets and crypto can make the same basket cheaper, flatter, or explosive depending on the chosen window.

02 · pick the nut

Price the world in nuts.

Choose a nut. Then convert dollars, gold, silver, platinum, and bitcoin into pounds of that nut using a real 2024 producer-price benchmark.

🌰 Almond standard
2024 U.S. producer benchmark · shelled edible portion · California
$2.14
per pound of the selected nut
2024 is the common benchmark year because producer-price tables, precious-metal annual averages, and a full bitcoin year can all be aligned to the same calendar year. USDA Crop Values Gold history BTC 2024
03 · read it clearly

What the conversion means.

A conversion into nuts is not a moral judgment. It is only a different unit of account. The question is simple: how much physical output does one unit buy?

same object
One basket

The CPI basket is held constant. Only the denominator changes.

more units required
weaker

If the basket needs more dollars or more nuts, that unit lost purchasing power against that basket.

fewer units required
stronger

If the basket needs less gold or less bitcoin, that unit gained purchasing power against that basket.

important limit
not total return

A raw commodity is not the same thing as a farm enterprise, land return, or a stock-market total return.

04 · the same basket, different money

Inflation changes when the ruler changes.

Below, the same CPI basket is expressed in four units. 2013 = 100. Above 100 means the basket became more expensive in that unit. Below 100 means it became cheaper in that unit.

Cost of the same CPI basket

BLS CPI-UUSDA almond historyGold historyCoin Metrics BTC
Interpretation: the U.S. CPI basket needed 34.7% more dollars in 2024 than in 2013. It needed about 102% more almonds, 20.4% less gold, and 99.6% less bitcoin. This is a worked example using almonds. Change the nut and the story changes.
05 · every nut is its own currency

No single nut standard exists.

Peanuts, almonds, macadamias, pecans, pistachios and walnuts each reflect different land, climate, labor, yield, storage and market conditions. Each one tells a different purchasing-power story.

2024 unitProducer price$20 buysPrice basis
“Nut” is used here as an economic category rather than strict botanical taxonomy. Peanuts are legumes; coconuts are drupes. The purchasing-power method still works the same way.
06 · make it visible

What the same $20 could buy.

These are simple historical purchasing-power snapshots using real producer or market prices. The baskets use emojis instead of carts to keep the comparison immediate.

08 · same clock

Put the nut complex on the same modern window.

Official BLS nut price indexes, all reset to December 1991 = 100. This is the cleanest same-clock answer to the question: which nut price indexes rose faster or slower than CPI?

What this says: there is no species-independent answer to “did nuts beat inflation?” In this exact BLS window, almond and hazelnut/filbert rose faster than CPI; pistachio, walnut, and peanut rose slower.
09 · producer ≠ commodity ≠ landowner

Three different things can move in three different directions.

A cheap nut does not automatically mean a bad orchard, and an expensive orchard does not automatically mean a profitable grower.

🌰

Nut price

The commodity itself can lose real value. Almond and peanut farm prices both lagged CPI over the long windows above. That is the price of the output, not the return on the farm.

BLS CPI-U
🧑‍🌾

Grower

Yield can improve while margins get squeezed. California almond yield rose from about 890 lb/ac in 1995 to about 1,980 lb/ac in 2024, but operating costs per acre rose sharply while the farm price fell.

UC cost studiesUSDA 2024 final
🗺️

Landowner

Water-secure land can appreciate even when the nut does not. In California almond land, Tier 1 surface-water districts rose from roughly $31k/ac to $40k/ac from 2018 to 2023, while Tier 2 groundwater districts stayed near $24k/ac.

UC ANR land study
The important distinction: the nut is a commodity; the grower owns a productive operation; the landowner owns a scarce productive asset. Their economics are connected, but they are not interchangeable.
10 · producer vs landowner

The nut can get cheaper while producing it gets more expensive.

Farm-gate price is only one line of the orchard balance sheet.

13 · the whole nut economy

The edible nut is only one output.

A serious Nut Standard has to count the rest of the biological and economic system: hulls, shells, trees, pollination, water, land, and secondary markets.

27 lb
Kernel — human food. This is the commodity price most people mean when they say “the almond price.”
19 lb
Shells — secondary material. Shells can return to soil, become biomass/biochar, or be converted into activated carbon.

14 · the full balance sheet

What a mature Nut Standard should measure.

Price alone is too small. A biological monetary standard needs the asset, the productive flow, the coproducts, and the risks in the same frame.

🌰

Commodity

Price / lb + volatility
What the edible output trades for and how unstable that price is.

🌳

Productivity

Yield / acre + orchard age
How much biological output the productive asset generates.

🐝

Pollination

Fee / acre + colony market
A separate service economy required by many nut crops.

💧

Water

Cost + rights + reliability
Both an operating input and a determinant of land value.

🗺️

Land

Value / acre + rent
The scarce productive asset underneath the crop.

♻️

Coproducts

Hulls + shells + wood + oils + meal
Secondary outputs that can become feed, materials, energy, or soil inputs.

🧑‍🌾

Operating economics

Labor + fertilizer + energy + harvest
The difference between a valuable crop and a profitable farm.

🌍

Ecological capital

Soil carbon + biomass + recycling
Whole-orchard recycling and biomass change what remains in the land after the crop.

BTC is converted at its yearly USD price; almonds use that year's USDA annual average grower price. The comparison is physical: pounds of almonds per BTC.
Physical purchasing power: this does not mean Bitcoin is a stable inflation hedge. It means that on the specified dates, BTC appreciated far faster than the USD price of this almond benchmark. BTC itself is highly volatile.
16 · source system

The Nut Standard is a reproducible data stack.

Primary sources stay attached to the figures they support. The dataset map is organized by economic layer so the standard can be extended instead of hand-waved.

core U.S. nut data

USDA ERS Fruit and Tree Nuts Yearbook, USDA NASS Crop Values, Quick Stats, and State historical nut reports provide price, yield, acreage, production, crop value, trade and supply context.

ERS yearbookCrop Values 2025 summary
inflation and external rulers

BLS CPI-U provides the consumer basket benchmark. BLS/FRED provides nut PPIs. Gold history reaches back to 1833. Bitcoin daily history begins in 2010. Shiller data extend the stock-market benchmark back to 1871.

BLS CPIProcessed nuts PPIShiller data
whole-system layers

UC Davis cost studies, UC ANR land and bioeconomy work, USDA pollination surveys, USDA ARS by-product research, and FAOSTAT/FAO producer-price systems extend the Nut Standard beyond the raw kernel price.

UC cost studiesFAOSTATFAO producer prices
A dollar is a unit. A nut is a unit. Gold is a unit. Land is a productive asset. The Nut Standard asks the same question of all of them: what can one unit buy, produce, or preserve over time?
17 · glossary

What every technical term means.

Each definition is tied to the official statistical or agricultural source used by the page. Terms are separated because a farm-gate price, a producer-price index, a consumer-price index, a retail price, and a land return are not the same measurement.

Processed nut prices · BLS PPI

What it is: a Producer Price Index for the nut-processing industry. It measures changes in selling prices received by U.S. producers/manufacturers, not raw farm prices and not grocery-store prices. On this page, it is the processed nuts and seeds industry series. BLS/FRED series BLS PPI definition

Producer Price Index · PPI

What it is: an index measuring the average change over time in selling prices received by domestic producers. It is a seller-side price measure. It is not the same thing as CPI. BLS

Consumer Price Index · CPI / CPI-U

What it is: the average change over time in prices paid by consumers for a representative basket of goods and services. CPI-U covers urban consumers and is the broad inflation benchmark used on this page. BLS CPI definition BLS coverage

CPI basket

What it is: the representative collection of consumer goods and services whose prices are tracked by BLS. Major groups include food, housing, apparel, transportation, medical care, recreation, education/communication, and other goods and services. BLS

Rebased index · “1998 = 100”

What it means: every series is rescaled so it starts at the same value, usually 100. A later reading of 187 means that series is 87% above its starting level. Rebasing changes the presentation, not the underlying percentage changes. BLS rebasing

Nominal value

What it means: the number of dollars without adjusting for inflation. $1 remains nominally $1 even if the amount of goods it can buy changes. CPI is commonly used to convert nominal values into inflation-adjusted values. BLS CPI as deflator

Real / inflation-adjusted value

What it means: a nominal value after adjusting for changes in the price level. On this page, “real” usually means adjusted using CPI-U unless another denominator is stated explicitly. BLS

Purchasing power

What it means here: how much of a chosen good, basket, or asset one unit can buy. If $1 buys fewer pounds of peanuts than before, the dollar lost purchasing power against peanuts. If one pound of peanuts buys less of the CPI basket, the peanut lost purchasing power against that basket. BLS purchasing power

Producer price / farm-gate price

What it is: the price received by farmers at the first point of sale, ideally where the commodity leaves the farm. It excludes post-farm transport, processing, wholesale, and retail margins. FAO producer prices FAO definition

Prices received by farmers

What it is: USDA's historical and current measure of prices farmers receive for commodities sold. It is a producer-side price, not a retail price. USDA historical bulletin

Prices Paid Index

What it is: USDA's measure of changes in prices paid by agricultural producers for production inputs and family living. It measures input-price change, not total production expenses, because quantities used can also change. USDA methodology

Wholesale price

What it is: a price in the distribution chain after production and before final retail. It may include transport, handling, storage, and wholesaler margins. A historical wholesale quote should not be compared directly with a farm-gate price without labeling the difference. FAO price layers

Retail price

What it is: the price paid by the final consumer. It includes costs and margins added after the farm gate, such as processing, packaging, transport, wholesale, and retail operations. FAO price layers

Yield per acre

What it is: physical crop output produced per acre in a season or year. It is a productivity measure. A lower price per pound can coexist with higher revenue per acre if yield rises enough. USDA ERS tree-nut data

Bearing acreage

What it is: acreage of mature orchards or trees currently producing a commercial crop. Non-bearing acreage consists of planted acreage not yet producing commercially. USDA ERS

Gross crop value per acre

What it means here: producer price × yield per acre. It measures gross output value before water, labor, fertilizer, pollination, machinery, insurance, interest, rent, and other costs. It is not profit. USDA ERS gross returns/acre

Operating cost per acre

What it is: variable and operating expenses required to produce the crop, such as labor, irrigation, fertilizer, pest management, machinery operations, harvest, and other recurring inputs. UC Davis publishes crop-specific cost-and-return studies. UC Davis

Breakeven price

What it is: the commodity price required for expected revenue to cover the defined cost base. A “full-cost” breakeven includes more costs than an operating-cost breakeven, so the cost definition must always be stated. UC Davis cost studies

Pollination fee / pollination-service receipts

What it is: payment from a grower to a beekeeper for colonies used to pollinate a crop. For the grower it is a production expense; for the beekeeper it is service revenue. USDA reports fees per colony, costs per acre, acreage, colonies, and total value. USDA Cost of Pollination

Land value / cropland value

What it is: the market value of agricultural real estate or cropland per acre. Statewide cropland value is a broad benchmark and should not be mistaken for a specific almond-orchard appraisal. USDA NASS Land Values

Cash rent

What it is: cash paid to rent agricultural land, usually reported per acre. A statewide irrigated-cropland rent combines many crop and land types and is therefore context, not an orchard-specific rent. USDA NASS Cash Rents

Co-product / by-product

What it means here: material produced alongside the primary edible nut. Examples include almond hulls and shells, peanut skins and shells, coconut husk/coir, copra meal, and cashew shell liquid. Whether value belongs to the grower, huller, processor, or another party depends on contracts and processing structure. UC ANR almond byproducts FAO cashew products

In-shell vs shelled / edible basis

Why it matters: an in-shell price is quoted on the weight of the nut plus shell, while a shelled or edible-kernel price is quoted on usable kernel weight. They are different units and cannot be compared directly without conversion. USDA ERS tree-nut tables

Total return

What it means here: all economic return from an asset over a period. For stocks this includes price appreciation plus dividends. For productive farmland it can include net farm cash flow or rent plus land appreciation. A raw nut-price change is not a total return. Shiller price + dividend data USDA returns concepts

Nut basket / Nut Standard index

What it is: a constructed index combining multiple nut species. Results depend on the weighting rule—equal weight, production weight, or crop-value weight—and the exact price layer used. The weighting rule must be stated explicitly. USDA ERS source data

Same-clock comparison

What it means: every asset or price series is measured over the exact same start and end dates. This removes one major source of distortion when comparing volatile commodities whose conclusions can change with the starting year. BLS index rebasing
